The prototype Astrocade that Perkins Engineering modified to go into commercial (hi-res) mode has been confirmed to still exist.  I have no other information than that right now (I don't even know if it still works).  Here are two parts of the announcement from the Arcadian newsletter that talks about the upgrade (it was supposed to be available in kit form; I don't know if it ever actually was available):

1) Announcment from: Arcadian, Vol. 3, No. 6, Pg. 63

A New Item from Perkins Engineering:

We are pleased to announce another engineering breakthrough - high resolution graphics.  The Hi-Rez Add-In from Perkins Engineering using 39 additional chips to exploit the high resolution capability of the Bally custom chips. 3296:
I talked to Mike White again over the weekend and learned a bit more
about Dave Ibach's tapes.

Game of Life isn't actually for the Assember.  You load it into
AstroBASIC with :RUN.  I'd actually tried this before and thought the
results were just glitches from the internal ROM (the fact that the
program's accompanied by a hideous buzz tended to promote this
perception).  It is actually playable if you use the right keys.  Mike
White wondered if this was Jay Fenton's Game of Life.  I tried it out
and they do actually seem about the same, except that the one we have
from the Jay Fenton tape has an introduction and none of the buzzing.
 So, this would appear to be a glitchy, machine-language-only version
of Jay Fenton's game.  Not the greatest find I could imagine, but
there you go.  :-)

The Honey Bear data assembled as a cartridge was confirmed to work,
but there is no actual game, just a series of options menus.  So,
perhaps this could be considered an extremely early cartridge
prototype, or maybe (as Mike speculated) it was just to show the
Assembler class how to make menus.

He also found a version of the Flying Witch program on the Halloween
Graphics tape which only runs for a minute or two before stopping.  I
think the regular version runs indefinitely.

This is probably about all Mike White's going to get from these tapes.
 There might be a bit more to discover, but someone with a RAM
expansion would have to put some time into investigating.  I was
hoping to find something more elaborate, but it's been interesting
nonetheless.

On a side note, Mike always has an Astrocade anecdote at the ready.
Once, he visited Bill Loos of L&M and saw a demonstration of the L&M
Interface and Light Show.  He could have bought it for $50, but he
didn't, and he says he's been kicking himself ever since!  I do
actually have some of the L&M Interface software.  (It's on-line with
the 300 baud programs.)  But I've never seen the interface that makes
it interact with your stereo.

Paul

I've ordered used books many times before, but I've never actually taken advantage of this service to get any books that have been out of print, so this has been kind of a learning experience for me.

If youve never order used books, then I highly recommend trying out Amazon.com.  In fact, if you have ANY interest in programming the Astrocade, then order "Programming the Z80" by Rodnay Zaks.  Amazon has a copy of it right now for just $6.44 (plus 3.49 shipping):

http://www.amazon.com/Programming-Z80-Rodnay-Zaks/dp/0895880695/sr=1-1/qid=1158622503/ref=sr_1_1/102-9669389-3588931?ie=UTF8&s=books

While searching for Z80 books, I found a neat service called Fetchbook (http://www.fetchbook.info).  You can enter a book and then it searches various databases (it claims 126 bookstores) looking for the book and the lowest price (the book need not be out of print).  Try it out!

It's pretty hard to find out what the z80 books online are about; there really aren't that many reviews for older books on Amazon.com (unless they are popular).  I've basically been ordering blind.  Any book with the word z80 in the title (that isn't WAY overpriced) is coming my way.  I've gotten quite a few books already, but I won't have time to look at ANY of them in other than a cursory manner for quite a while.

While searching for recommended Z80 books I ran into a Sinclair Spectrum website that highly recommended a book called "Spectrum Machine Language for the Absolute Beginner."  There was a review of the book and it said that there was a Frogger-type game in it.  Now, I've got probably a dozen Z80 programming books and NONE of them cover games at all; THAT'S what interests me.  I checked Amazon.com for the book, but it didn't come up at all.  I checked Amazon.co.uk, and the book was there for 5.50 pounds, plus 6.94 pounds international shipping (12.44, total).  You can check out the book here:

http://www.amazon.co.uk/Spectrum-Machine-Language-Absolute-Beginner/dp/0861611101/sr=8-2/qid=1158622280/ref=sr_1_2/202-4899875-5102262?ie=UTF8&s=gateway

I went ahead and ordered the book; I let my credit card figure-out how much 12.44 pounds are in US funds (it's about $20).

Today, after only seven days, I received "Spectrum Machine Language for the Absolute Beginner."  (Ive been getting a book a day for about a week now).  I quickly skimmed the book; it brings a smile to my face.  The other Z80 books that I own are aimed at serious programming, and if there is a figure in them, then it is technical (i.e. boring).  This book has drawings of little elves with CPU-bodies through-out it.  I'm not sure what I can LEARN from an elf, but it means that the book isn't going to be showing fiteen different kinds of sorts.  When I looked at the book, I was immediately reminded of books by Compute! for the Atari and C64 (to my knowledge Compute never wrote a book for a Z80 computer did they?).  The included Frogger-type game, called Freeway Frog, has a screen-shot (actually its obviously a printout of a screen capture; very old school!).  The game looks neat (well, ITS Frogger).  The source for the game is thirty-six pages (with another thirty-one pages that explains how it all works!).

My bet is that somewhere out on the net Ill find a compiled version of Freeway Frog that I can play on a Spectrum emulator.  My experience with the Spectrum is practically zero; Ive spent a few hours with emulation, but it never pulled me in; maybe this will give me an excuse to try it out.

Once I get more of the Z80 books, Ill share a list of everything that I get and maybe say a few words about them.

Some more details :

The code runs on the $150 Xilinx Spartan3e starter kit. You will need
to add a few resistors to get some more colours, and add a
resistor/cap to get audio output. You can imagine an expansion board
which had these additions and some joystick connectors although I have
not got time for that at the moment - although I would modify the VHDL
code if someone else did it.

You can download the bally.bit file to the board over USB using the
Xilinx Impact tool (all this is in the board documentation) and it
will boot up. The code uses the on board flash for cartridges, and you
can program the flash over an rs232 cable. I downloaded Treasure Cove
to the flash and it worked fine. I have wired up two of the on board
switches to bits 14&13 of the flash so you can switch between 4 carts.
Clearly you could have many more and add some logic to switch from a
menu for example.

The hi-res mode switches on the hi-res register just like the real chips.

The RAM is from 0x4000 - 0xBFFF (28K) 0x0000-0x3FFF is mirrored to
0x4000-0x7FFF for the magic write stuff.

I will run up a hi-res test program and take pics if anybody wishes to
send one.

Cheers,

The Custom DATA chip overheats extremely easy. If you happen to block the bottom vents on the Arcade (like buy putting it on a rug or towel,etc.), the air flow isn't enough to keep the chip cool. This chip CAN be reproduced in a better manner, but it is much better to just remake the whole thing, all 30 chips (33 in the original) including the one in the rf modulator, into one chip that doesn't have the problem of overheating. Your unit will be fine if you can keep it cool. a small fan on ti works good, as well as placing it on a hard, smooth surface.
The biggest problem is that the custom DATA chips are no longer available. They haven't been made for almost 2 decades.

Adam and others have made good points.

Clearly, what we have been doing is more than just for a collector
who can go out and eBay a finite amount of working BPA's.

We are very, very close to getting what we want. All that needs to
be done is to use a simple ADC, Analog-to-Digital-Convertor to allow
for the paddle inputs.

Everything else is done.

Now, we could use the schematic for the Blue RAM. I have sent Mike J
the docs on the special chip that product uses. Also, what is the
circuit for the AstroBasic tape input/output?

But think about this. We're almost there. Clearly, the Spartan 3e
board is good for hackers and experimenters, but not for the average
person. That's fine.

You see, we have a couple of venues to pursue to get a replacement
board. The first is to use the XSA-200, since it uses a Spartan FPGA
and port the code Mike J has done into it. What we would need to do
is create a daughter board that it would connect to that would have
the auido, 4 joystick ports, and the cartridge port. Simple enough.
The XSA doesn't have a dual-channel ADC like the Spartan 3e starter
board does but what we need is fairly simple. But, the XSA has 9-
bits of color for 512 colors. Plenty for what we need. (The XSA-200
has 83 pins of I/O versus 43 on the Spartan 3e FX2 port)

That would be the easiest design. As it would use the XSA-200 for
the grunt work. Design and layout, including costs, would be lower.

The second venue is actually already available to use. You see, both
the XSA-200 AND the Spartan 3e starter board include plenty of 
system schematics. We'd only take what we'd need and layout the
board. Problem is-PCB layout costs and total component costs may be
greater than the previous venue. But, it is an option-again-the
schematics already exist!

If I remember correctly, a certain member here has already made
their PCB layout skills known.

If the schematic for the Blue RAM can be made known, and the special
chip simulated in VHDL, then all we need is a daughter board to the
XSA-200 to get what we want.

Finally, I have been talking to Mike White and Kenn Lill. We can get
the high-res unit-but all we actually need is the EPROM, a 4K, that
changes the BPA bios. Once that is dumped, we can send that to Mike
J for testing on the VHDL BPA high-res unit. We also have the
schematics for the high-res unit too!

The high-res BASIC is a tape image though. Guys, any comments on how
to preserve it?

It may be a strecth, but we could do a replacement motherboard
layout that would only need an XSA-200 to run the whole thing. Sans
RF modulator and flaky custom chip operation!

And, if carefully asked, we could also have Blue RAM operation!

What do you all think?

Jim

The serial ports are buffered to the extent that the VCS would
actually be able to use them efficiently for interfacing with
alternate controllers or for multiplayer networking.

For instance, the 2600 had limited ability to read trackballs in
proportional mode.  It just isn't fast enough.  It barely works for
Thomas' Missile Command hack.  One use of the serial ports would be
to interface with older serial/combo trackballs or through a PS2
adapter to modern trackballs.  It could also use keyboards.

> what is the purpose of them for a general user?

Initially, the end-user who is not a programmer can use it like a
multicart.  Its initial goal is Supercharger compatibility.  It is a
replacement Supercharger on steroids.  And it would be at a
pricepoint much lower than a Cuttle Cart 1 or 2, and readily
available in quantities rather than scouring Ebay.  The end-user can
also (down the line) play any new games which use the newer features,
although we'd also like to offer the cart as a platform for
homebrewers to distribute their finished games preloaded.  So some
people might wind up with a Chimera just by virtue of buying a
finished homebrew, which they can then "unlock".

>what can 
> the RISC processor be used for besides controlling the ports?
Could it
> actually be used in conjunction with the 6509?  Now THAT would be
WEIRD.

I think you mean 6507.

The ARM is actually there because it's more of a package deal.  The
ARM contains two serial ports and a flash memory controller.  If we
didn't use that chip, we'd spend MORE money using a bigger CPLD or
FPGA to do it, or more support chips.  If we didn't come up with more
stuff for the ARM to do, it would be largely wasted outside of
loading games since the CPLD does most of the work.

So we intend to allow programmers to run small custom ARM subroutines
in addition to calling a few select routines built into the
firmware.  We're trying to get it so that the ARM can run in parallel
with the VCS so that the 6507 won't necessarily have to sit there
waiting for the routine to finish.  Although there is 128K of SRAM,
the ARM has a realtively slow method of accessing it, and it can't
run ARM code from there.  It has to run from its internal 8K and or
32K flash firmware area.  That's why we're trying to work out some
useful built-in functions now since the firmware area is not really
meant to be overwritten with each new game load.  It really has to be
like the Bally has a lot of built in helper routines.

Besides loading games and working with the ports, the ARM's main task
right now is to service queues.  Queues are arrays of memory exposed
to the VCS through 1-byte access windows.  You might also want to
call them stacks or circular buffers.  This is similar to what David
Crane has in the DPC in Pitfall II.  This way of accessing data is
the most efficient way to prepare graphics for a kernel on the VCS.

During VBLANK, then you could start to call special ARM functions.
There are 16 queues in the internal ARM RAM.  These are intended to
be used for pseudo-bitmaps.  So we hope to offer some canned bitmap
kernels (or graphics modes if you want to call them that) and you
will be able to call special generic drawing functions for the ARM.
The ARM should be fast enough to insure that the work completes by
the time the next frame starts.  These modes are going to be pretty
flickery and maybe not too colorful, but outside of that, some cool
things will be possible.

Astrocade

coprocessor, and while I like Richard Hutchinson's stuff, he never
went whole hog in letting the Vectrex use the serial port.  I think
the 2600 is probably the hardest environment for this because of the
limitations of that cart port.

3414:
Classic Gaming Books

I've read a couple of classic gaming books over the past few of months (only one of them mentions the Astrocade).  The books are:

1)  The Ultimate History of Video Games by Steven L. Kent - You've probably heard of this.  After I read this book I was pretty excited about how good it was.  There are just TONS of quotes in this book.  My only problem with this book is that it is held together by the quotes a little TOO much.  The author doesnt use the quotes to enhance the book, rather the book is held together with the quotes.  Often Kent gives a summary of a quote, and then gives you the quote.  He should do one or the other but not BOTH.  Still, this is a very fine book.  This book does talk (briefly) about the Bally Arcade.

2)  On the Edge, The Spectacular Rise and Fall of Commodore by Brian Bangnall - The best book that I've ever read on computer history.  Ever.  Period.  The only thing is it is Commodore specific.  Still, I KNEW that before I began.  This book just AMAZED me.  This author comes across more as a disinterested journalist than as a major fan of Commodore (thats how it SHOULD be).  Sometimes he DID let his enthusiasm slip through a bit, but it never hurt the material.

Then there are these books that I bought recently that I glance through at my computer once in a while:

3) Collectible Microcomputers by Michael Nadeau - I thought that this book was going to have more history, but its VERY thin there.  Its mostly got pictures of SO MANY COMPUTERS.  I never knew that there ever were so many different computers models made by SO many manufacturers.  The book is easily worth it for the pictures.  You cant so much read this book as flip through it time and time again looking for something new to capture your eye.  This has worked for me each time.

4) Digital Retro by Gordon Laing  This book does have more information than the above book, but it too is mostly just (super high quality!) pictures.  Ive not read much of the content as some reviews of this book say that there are many errors but then go on to say that the book is worth it for the pictures.  I agree with them about the pictures.  I didnt realize that this book was going to be about European computers and consoles, which makes it all the better for me.

On the day that I finished the Commodore book, yesterday, I received two other books in the mail that will become my new bathroom reading material:

5) Bill Kunkels Confessions of the Game Doctor by Bill Kunkel - This is a collection of material that Bill wrote for various places online with some additional new material added to it (to me, this is all new).  In the introduction by Arnie Katz, he calls this Bills memoirs; I dont know if that is true.  So far Ive only read Arnies introduction where he talks about meeting Bill in 1970 (though they had corresponded because of fandom magazines for a few years).  The introduction alone gave me SO much information that I never knew.  I expect this book to be pretty good.

6) Videogames in the Beginning by Ralph H. Baar  I couldnt resist this book.  I know quite a bit about Mr. Baar now that Ive read The Ultimate History of Video Games, but this is a BOOK by the man himself.  I havent read this yet, but there are a TON of pictures (many in color).  In fact, the pictures are worth the price of admission.  If Baar writes like he speaks in The Ultimate History of Video Games, then this book is going to be fun!

Has anyone else read these books?  Does anyone have any other books to recommend (besides Hackers, which I hope everyone reading this has read already!)?

Adam

Bally/Home Library Computer

Original 1977 Name. Keyboard add-on/under was to arrive shortly.

Production delays, changes in management, and the desire to appeal to a larger market resulted in:

Bally/Professional Arcade

If you were using the Blue Ram Utility 3.0 with the Blue Ram you would use the "DIAG" function.  Here's a description from the manual:

DIAG - Verifies the size of your Blue Ram and tests all memory components in the Blue Ram for proper operation.

I can't remember if this utility works with the Viper; try it and get back to us.

The Blue Ram Utility is a very capable and powerful program.  Among its many features: it allows you to program directly in Hex (EDIT), it prints a block of memory to the printer (LIST), it burns an EPROM (BURN), it disassembles a machine language program (DASM), it uses the modem to send and receive programs (SEND and RECV), it will automatically put a "fresh" copy of itself on tape (DUMP), it will move a program to the cartridge area so that it can be run exactly like a cartridge (TEST), it can copy a cartridge to tape (COPY, SAVE, LOAD and VRFY) and the utility is capable of quite a few other tasks too.  As you can see from just the few functions mentioned, you could actually create cartridges with this program!

If you're interested in reading the whole Blue Ram Utility Manual 3.0 (which is only three pages long), then you can read it here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/perkins/docs-blue_ram_utility3.pdf

Reading this the Blue Ram Utility manual gives you an idea of just how capable the Astrocade actually was: it wasnt just a game machine!
